grammar_topic: word order in questions; present simple
title: Five Minutes to Decide
body: At the speed-dating event, every couple has exactly five minutes together before a bell rings. 'What do you do at the weekends?' Aziz asks the woman across the table. 'I paint,' she says, 'and I never miss my Sunday run.' She seems confident and funny, and Aziz likes her immediately. 'Where do you usually go on holiday?' she asks him back. 'I don't travel much,' he admits, 'but I love cooking for my friends.' The bell rings before they finish talking, and Aziz moves to the next table, disappointed. Ten conversations later, he still thinks about her answers. At the end of the evening, the organizer reads out the matches. 'Table four and table nine — you both chose each other!' Aziz laughs with relief; table nine was exactly the woman with the Sunday run. He finally has her number, and this time there's no bell to stop the conversation.

title: The Renovation Show
body: Every Friday, millions of people watch 'Home Makeover' on television. The show usually follows the same pattern: a family lives in an old, tired house, and two designers arrive with big plans. This week, the Karimov family is standing in their garden, watching workers carry furniture out of the house. 'We're renovating the kitchen and the bathroom,' explains the lead designer, 'and we're also painting every room a different colour.' The family doesn't usually spend much money on their home, so they're a little nervous. Right now, one worker is knocking down an old wall, while another is measuring the new kitchen island. By the end of the episode, the house always looks completely different. The Karimovs are currently living with relatives, but they're counting the days until they can move back. 'I can't believe we're doing this,' says Mrs. Karimov, smiling at the camera. 'Our house never looks this exciting.'

title: The Power Cut
body: Last Tuesday, the whole neighbourhood lost electricity at exactly eight o'clock. Malika was cooking dinner when the lights suddenly went out. She lit two candles and continued chopping vegetables in the dark kitchen. Meanwhile, her neighbours were sitting outside, talking and laughing under the stars. Her brother, who was studying for an exam, complained loudly about his laptop battery. 'I finished my homework just in time,' he said, closing the lid. The power stayed off for almost three hours. While they waited, the family played cards by candlelight, something they hadn't done in years. Malika finally served dinner at half past ten, much later than usual. 'At least the food didn't get cold,' she joked, since the stove used gas, not electricity. When the lights finally came back on, nobody rushed to turn on the television. They just sat there for a moment, blinking in the sudden brightness, strangely sorry that the evening was over.

grammar_topic: past simple; time sequencers and connectors
title: The Longest Bus Ride
body: First, the bus left the station twenty minutes late. Then, after only an hour, it stopped at the side of the road with a flat tyre. While the driver changed the wheel, all the passengers got out to stretch their legs. Suddenly, it started raining, so everyone ran back inside. Afterwards, the bus continued for two more hours until it reached a small town for a break. Farrukh bought bread and tea at a roadside stall before the driver called everyone back. Eventually, as the sun began to set, the bus climbed into the mountains, and the road became narrow and winding. Finally, just before midnight, the bus arrived at the final stop, six hours later than planned. Despite the delay, Farrukh didn't feel angry. Instead, he felt strangely proud, as if he had survived a small adventure. As soon as he stepped off the bus, his cousin ran over and hugged him. 'You made it!' she laughed. 'Next time, take the train.'

words.context: It stopped with a flat tyre.
...to stretch their legs.

grammar_topic: be going to; present continuous (future arrangements)
title: The Wedding Plan
body: Nigora is getting married in June, and she's already planning every detail. 'We're having the ceremony in my grandmother's garden,' she tells her friend, showing photos on her phone. 'And my cousin is bringing the flowers from her shop.' She's going to wear her mother's old wedding dress, which a tailor is currently altering. Her fiancé, Bekzod, isn't worried about the details; he's simply going to trust Nigora's plans completely. 'I'm meeting the photographer on Thursday,' Nigora continues, 'and we're choosing the menu with the restaurant next week.' Her friend asks if she's nervous. 'A little,' Nigora admits, 'but mostly I'm excited.' She's going to invite almost two hundred guests, which seems like a lot, but weddings in her family are always huge. Bekzod is picking up the rings tomorrow morning, and after that, there's really nothing left to organize except waiting for June to arrive.

words.context: We're having the ceremony in my grandmother's garden.
A tailor is currently altering it.

grammar_topic: defining relative clauses; be going to
title: The Perfect Flat
body: Jamshed is looking for a flat that's close to his office and doesn't cost too much money. The agent, who has shown him five apartments already, calls with one more option. 'It's a flat that has a small balcony and a kitchen that just got renovated,' she explains. Jamshed, who hates wasting time, agrees to see it immediately. The building, which was built only two years ago, looks modern and clean. Inside, he meets the owner, a woman who works as a teacher nearby. 'This is the room where I keep my books,' she says, showing him around. Jamshed likes the flat that overlooks a quiet street with trees. 'I'm going to think about it tonight,' he tells the agent, though he already knows the answer. The neighbours, who he briefly meets in the hallway, seem friendly enough. By the next morning, Jamshed is going to sign the contract for the flat that finally feels like home.

words.context: The agent calls with one more option.

title: Not Everything Yet
body: We've just moved into our new apartment, and boxes are still everywhere. 'Have you unpacked the kitchen yet?' my mother asks over the phone. 'I've already finished the kitchen,' I tell her, 'but I haven't touched the bedroom yet.' My brother has already hung the pictures in the living room, though nothing matches on the walls. 'Have you found the coffee machine yet?' he asks, clearly missing his morning coffee. 'Not yet,' I admit, 'it's probably still in one of these boxes.' We've already met one neighbour, an elderly man who has already brought us a plate of biscuits. I haven't seen the whole building yet, but I've already noticed how quiet the street is. My mother asks if we've registered our new address yet. 'We haven't done that yet,' I confess, 'but we'll go tomorrow.' Slowly, box by box, this empty apartment is already starting to feel like ours.

words.context: Have you unpacked the kitchen yet?

grammar_topic: present perfect or past simple (1); something, anything, nothing
title: Still Waiting to Hear
body: Sitora had her job interview three days ago, but she hasn't heard anything from the company yet. 'Did they say when they'd call?' her flatmate asks. 'They said they'd call by Friday,' Sitora replies, 'but nothing has happened so far.' Yesterday, she checked her email ten times, hoping for something, anything, but there was nothing in her inbox except adverts. She has already applied to two other companies, just in case. Last week, she felt confident after the interview; the manager smiled a lot and asked detailed questions about her experience. Now, she isn't sure if that meant anything at all. Her flatmate has been through this before and has some advice. 'I once waited two whole weeks for an answer,' she says, 'and it turned out fine.' Sitora nods, though it doesn't help much right now. She hasn't told her parents about the interview yet, in case there's nothing to tell. She decides to wait until tomorrow before calling the company herself.

words.context: Her flatmate asks about the interview.

Nothing except adverts.

title: Two Cafés, One Street
body: On the same street, there are two small cafés, and everyone in town has an opinion about them. The café on the corner is cheaper than the one opposite, but its coffee isn't as strong as its rival's. The waiters there are friendlier, though the tables are smaller and closer together. Across the street, the newer café looks more modern, with bigger windows and softer music. Its cakes are more expensive, but customers say they're worth it. 'This coffee is just as good as the one in the capital,' an old man tells his friend, tapping the table proudly. The corner café is busier in the mornings, while the modern one fills up faster in the evenings. Prices there are higher, but the service is quicker. Some people are more loyal to one café than the other, arguing for hours about which is truly better. Personally, I think both cafés are as important to this street as the old clock tower nearby.

grammar_topic: superlatives (+ ever + present perfect); quantifiers: too, not enough
title: The Best Meal I've Ever Had
body: 'This is the best meal I've ever eaten in this city,' Dilnoza says, putting down her fork. The restaurant, hidden in a small side street, is the quietest place she's ever found for dinner. 'It's also the cheapest of the three restaurants we've tried this month,' her husband adds. The portions are generous, though some dishes are too spicy for their daughter, who prefers milder food. 'There isn't enough sauce for the rice,' the little girl complains, pushing her plate slightly. The waiter, the most patient one they've ever met, brings extra sauce without being asked twice. 'This is definitely the friendliest restaurant we've visited,' Dilnoza's husband says, looking around at the busy tables. Dilnoza has never had such fresh bread before, still warm from the oven. There isn't enough time to try dessert tonight, but she's already planning her next visit. 'We should come back,' she says. 'This might be the best discovery we've made all year.'

words.context: The portions are generous.

title: The Weather Forecaster's Bet
body: Our local weather forecaster, Umar, makes a bold prediction every morning on the radio. 'It won't rain today,' he announces confidently, 'and the sky will stay clear until evening.' His listeners have learned not to trust him completely, since he's often wrong. Today, within an hour, dark clouds appear, and by lunchtime, it's raining heavily. 'This will pass quickly,' Umar insists on air, though the storm continues for the rest of the afternoon. His colleagues joke that if Umar predicts sunshine, everyone should bring an umbrella. 'Tomorrow will definitely be warmer,' he promises the next day, and for once, he's right. The office football team, half-serious, will bet a coffee on his forecasts every Friday. This week, Umar owes three coffees already. 'I won't give up,' he laughs, checking the satellite images again. 'One day, this city will finally trust my forecasts.' Until then, most people will simply carry an umbrella, just in case.

grammar_topic: will / won't / shall (other uses); review of verb forms
title: Shall We Surprise Her?
body: 'Shall we organize a surprise party for grandma's birthday?' Malika asks her brothers. 'I'll book the restaurant,' says the eldest, already reaching for his phone. 'I won't tell her anything, I promise,' laughs the youngest, who usually can't keep a secret. Their grandmother has celebrated many birthdays before, but this year will be different — the whole family is coming, even relatives from abroad. 'Shall I bake the cake, or will you order one?' Malika asks her sister. They decide together: she'll bake it, since grandma always says shop cakes won't taste as good as homemade ones. Yesterday, they walked past a shop, and grandma admired a blue scarf — that will be part of her present. On the day itself, everyone will hide in the garden until she arrives home from her walk. 'Will she really be surprised?' the youngest asks nervously. 'She's suspected nothing so far,' Malika reassures him. Soon, the whole family will shout 'Surprise!' together, and grandma won't stop smiling all evening.
